We learned yesterday that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed, accusing Apple's Photos app of violating state privacy laws through its facial recognition feature.

The case has been repeatedly conflated with Meta's use of facial recognition, even though the two companies' practices sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum. The judge's decision to let the case proceed shows the courts fundamentally do not understand how the feature works...

The earlier allegations against Meta

To properly understand the current situation, we need to start with a facial recognition lawsuit against Meta that dates back to 2015.

Because that facial recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta could identify those faces, the company did break the law and rightly had to settle for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under that same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which says companies cannot collect biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is completely different

There's a small problem with the accusation: Apple absolutely did not collect biometric data to perform facial recognition in its Photos app. As the company pointed out in a machine learning research paper it published in 2021, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

More than that, all the iPhone is doing is saying "these photos appear to be of the same person" — it has absolutely no idea who that person is. Only the iPhone user themselves can put a name to those faces.

Apple's privacy policy regarding Photos echoes this point.

It's astonishing that this lawsuit has now entered its sixth year of legal proceedings; it takes just a few minutes of research to show the claims are clearly unfounded.

Courts and legislatures should be actively praising Apple's approach to privacy, rather than lumping it in with companies like Meta that trample all over it.

This is yet another example of courts and legislatures fundamentally not understanding the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example is, of course, end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or tried to ban end-to-end encryption despite having no understanding of how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every field they touch. But they have access to experts, and what I find baffling is that these fundamentally flawed lawsuits and legislative attempts have apparently gone unchallenged for years.
